title: Hosea 10:9–15
context: Hosea 10:9–15 returns to the LORD’s own words. Israel has sinned since the days of Gibeah, and he will discipline them when he chooses, gathering nations against them. The two transgressions of verse 10 are not explained, and identifications are held loosely. Ephraim is a trained heifer that loves to thresh, but the LORD will put a yoke on her neck; Judah and Jacob will plow. Then comes a call: "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD, until he comes and rains righteousness on you" (compare Jeremiah 4:3). Yet Israel has plowed wickedness, eaten the fruit of lies, and trusted in its own way and its warriors. A battle roar will come, and fortresses will be destroyed as Shalman destroyed Beth Arbel; the identity of Shalman and the location of Beth Arbel are uncertain. Bethel will bring this on them, and Israel’s king will be cut off at dawn. Shared ground: both traditions read the call to seek the LORD as a sincere invitation set within a warning of judgment, and they treat the violence of verse 14 soberly.

verses.text: “Israel, you have sinned from the days of Gibeah. There they remained. The battle against the children of iniquity doesn’t overtake them in Gibeah.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Israel has sinned since the days of Gibeah, and there they remained. Arminian readers see a long history of sin going back to the time of the judges, which Israel never truly left behind.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reference to Judges 19–21 as showing the persistence of Israel’s corruption. Both traditions note that the second half of the verse is difficult and read in different ways, and they hold it loosely.

verses.text: When it is my desire, I will chastise them; and the nations will be gathered against them when they are bound to their two transgressions.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will discipline them when he desires, and nations will gather against them for their two transgressions. Arminians see God’s discipline following Israel’s persistent sin, carried out through foreign nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign timing in judgment. Both traditions note that the two transgressions are not explained; some suggest the two calves or the double sin of idolatry and kingship, and they hold the question open.

verses.text: Ephraim is a trained heifer that loves to thresh, so I will put a yoke on her beautiful neck. I will set a rider on Ephraim. Judah will plow. Jacob will break his clods.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Ephraim is a trained heifer that loves to thresh, but he will yoke her neck, and Judah and Jacob will plow. Arminian readers see the easy work of threshing contrasted with the harder labor of plowing that judgment brings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing God’s discipline. Both traditions note that threshing heifers were allowed to eat as they worked (compare Deuteronomy 25:4), and they read the yoke as a picture of hardship.

verses.text: Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to kindness. Break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD, until he comes and rains righteousness on you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls them to sow righteousness, reap kindness, and break up fallow ground, for it is time to seek him until he rains righteousness on them. Arminians see a sincere invitation to repentance, which shows that God still offers his people a way back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the invitation is sincere and see the righteousness God rains as his gift. Both traditions compare Jeremiah 4:3, and they hold the call to seek the LORD as shared ground.

verses.text: You have plowed wickedness. You have reaped iniquity. You have eaten the fruit of lies, for you trusted in your way, in the multitude of your mighty men.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they plowed wickedness, reaped iniquity, and ate the fruit of lies, trusting their own way and warriors. Arminian readers see the people choosing the opposite of what God invited, with predictable results.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see self-trust as the root of their failure. Both traditions read the verse as the contrast to verse 12, showing what Israel sowed instead of righteousness.

verses.text: Therefore a battle roar will arise among your people, and all your fortresses will be destroyed, as Shalman destroyed Beth Arbel in the day of battle. The mother was dashed in pieces with her children.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says a battle roar will rise, fortresses will be destroyed as Shalman destroyed Beth Arbel, and mothers and children were crushed. Arminians receive this verse soberly, naming the horror of war without elaboration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a grim warning of judgment. Both traditions note that Shalman’s identity and Beth Arbel’s location are uncertain, and they read the verse with grief.

verses.text: So Bethel will do to you because of your great wickedness. At daybreak the king of Israel will be destroyed.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Bethel will bring this on them because of their great wickedness, and Israel’s king will be cut off at dawn. Arminian readers see judgment coming from the very place of false worship, which became the source of ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the irony that Bethel, house of God, brought destruction. Both traditions read the end of the king as the end of the northern monarchy, which came with Assyria’s conquest.
